title: Introduction to Architecture
description: ARCH1001 explores creative process, the realms of imagination, and design practices in viewing, experiencing, reading, and ultimately producing architectural FORM. Skills of ideation, representation and fabrication are developed in the context of each student’s capacity to observe, interpret and translate design concepts into physical form.
outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:   1. Demonstrate Foundational Technical Control and Perceptual Skills.  Through a curated portfolio containing orthographic projections (plan, section), paraline drawings (axonometric, plan oblique), and tonal studies (illuminated-volume drawings) that adhere to conventional architectural graphic standards.   2. Generate Architectural Form and Spatial Propositions Through Iterative Making. By producing a series of developmental sketch models and corresponding drawings that explore multiple spatial solutions from a given set of constraints (e.g., the "Eisenman" exercise).   3. Analyze and Articulate Spatial Conditions Through Critical Drawing Techniques.  Through analytical drawings—including serial sections, exploded axonometrics, and conceptual (parti) diagrams—that deconstruct and explain the formal, spatial, and experiential logic of both found and invented environments.   4. Synthesize Conceptual, Technical, and Contextual Knowledge into a Coherent Design Intervention.  Through a final project that integrates precedent analysis, principles of human scale and movement, and material tectonics into a resolved architectural proposition.   5. Critically Curate and Present a Design Process as a Structured Architectural Argument  By assembling and presenting a final portfolio that selectively sequences work from the semester to construct a clear narrative of learning and design thinking.
syllabus: Each “class” is a studio session – a workshop where the specific issues and methods will be worked “hands-on.”  Group projects, individual assignments, critiques, discussions, research and studio sessions will provide students an opportunity to work through issues and ideas within a social, cultural and personal context. The works are intended to serve as a basis for learning by observation, experimentation, and discovery.

title: Understanding Cities
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH2111.
description: This course introduces fundamental ways of understanding a city by looking at its architecture and physical environment as sites of collective living, production, exchange and consumption. From the production of art to the collection of rubbish, the course aims to explore the architectural and urban dimensions of cities (from material to cultural and symbolic) through salient topics such as city and war, city and power, city and trade, energy, transportation, housing, and entertainment. Referring to prominent cities in the world including Hong Kong, we will touch on significant urban themes such as local / global, memory / envisioning, development / sustainability. Topics include: What is a city for? How do cities work? How are cities made and remade? What role do architects and others play in the design, planning, maintenance and imagining of cities?
outcome: - a basic understanding of the way cities work in terms of their architectural and physical aspects  - an awareness of central themes of urban culture and their built manifestations  - an ability to discuss and formulate points of view on important urban issues by reference to appropriate cases  - fundamental skills to transfer the issues presented to other cities and cultures
syllabus: This course introduces fundamental ways of understanding a city by looking at its architecture and physical environment as sites of collective living, production, exchange and consumption. Important historical and contemporary examples will be used to explain the city through its layers. From the production of art to the collection of rubbish, the course aims to explore the architectural and urban dimensions of cities (from material to cultural and symbolic) through salient topics such as city and war, city and power, city and trade, energy, circulation (transportation), housing, entertainment (pleasure and sin), etc.   Referring to Hong Kong as well as other prominent cities in the world, we will touch on significant urban issues such as those between local / global, memory / envisioning, development / sustainability. Through lectures, seminars and group discussions, we will consider these topics by asking key questions such as: What is a city for? How do cities work? How are cities made and remade? What role do architects and others play in the design, planning, maintenance and imagining of cities?  This course aims to provide students with: a basic understanding of the way cities work in terms of their architectural and physical aspects; an awareness of central themes of urban culture and their built manifestations; an ability to discuss and formulate points of view on important urban issues by reference to appropriate cases.

title: Visual Studies
description: ARCH1003 is a foundational course in the instrumental language of architecture. Its primary focus is developing technical proficiency, manual craft, and representational clarity through a series of structured exercises. Students will master core conventions—such as line weight, orthographic projection, axonometric analysis, and model construction—to produce precise, communicative, and well-crafted drawings and physical models. This disciplined practice establishes the necessary groundwork for the parallel design studio. While the act of drawing is inherently a mode of thinking, the emphasis here is on acquiring the essential skills that will enable and elevate that thinking. The course operates on the principle that a robust command of representation is a prerequisite for effective design exploration and communication.
outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:   1. Employ observational and analytical drawing techniques to document and interrogate existing conditions. Generate a series of freehand sketches, photographs, and collages that move from descriptive recording to analytical dissection, identifying key formal, spatial, and tectonic qualities of a subject.   2. Demonstrate technical proficiency in architectural graphic conventions. Produce orthographic drawing sets (plans, sections, elevations) that accurately deploy standardized line weights, notations, and sheet composition to clearly delineate spatial boundaries, materiality, and hierarchy.   3. Construct and utilize paraline drawings as a tool for three-dimensional spatial analysis. Produce axonometric projections that actively dissect an object or assembly, using drawing techniques like cutaway, explosion, or highlight to reveal interior relationships, structural logic, or construction sequence.   4. Fabricate precise physical models to explore and communicate massing, scale, and assembly. Construct a series of study models, evolving from a unitary massing model to a detailed assembly model, demonstrating control of materials, tools, craft, and the intentional use of abstraction to convey specific architectural ideas.   5. Synthesize a range of representational techniques into a coherent visual argument. Assemble a final, structured drawing set (combining technical and freehand drawings) and corresponding model photography that presents a single subject through multiple, complementary lenses, demonstrating an integrated understanding of appropriate representational choice, scale, and presentation craft.
syllabus: This foundational course builds essential visual and tactile literacy for architectural communication. Over the course, students progressively master core techniques through focused modules. The sequence begins with observational skills - Phase1: photographic and freehand documentation), establishing a basis for accurate seeing. Phase2 concentrates on technical orthographic drawing, emphasizing line weight, notation, and craft. Analytical skills are developed through axonometric drawing and the introduction of collage as a multi-media representational tool  - Phase3. The course culminates in three-dimensional exploration, with students constructing sequential massing and assembly models, and learning professional model photography (Phase4). Each module delivers a specific, assessed output, ensuring the cumulative development of a precise, versatile skill set directly applicable to the parallel design studio.

title: Experiencing Architecture
requirements: Not for students who have taken UGEC1016 and ARCH2111.
description: (UGEC1016 is double-coded with ARCH1320.) The course provides a general outline to architecture. The aim is to introduce architecture as a cultural phenomenon. The course will increase the student's awareness of the built environment as it exists all around. It examines a variety of spatial experiences encountered in exemplary places and buildings. The scope of the course is not limited to buildings alone, but includes cities and landscapes as extensions of architecture. The course introduces a range of topics, including the historical, symbolic, aesthetic, functional, cultural and green aspects of architecture.

title: Introduction to Architectural Design I
description: Introduction to Architectural Design I to II and Architectural Design Studio I to IV (ARCH2111, 2112, 3113, 3114, 4115, 4116) form a sequence of project-based professional courses in architecture.Studio 1 – MEASURE (ARCH2111) focuses on cultivating a sophisticated understanding of architecture and its broader contextual built environment, beginning with the simple act of measuring. Measuring in this studio is considered the fundamental tool in establishing a direct relationship between our body and the surrounding physical environment. Through measuring, students will be introduced to a series of architectural concepts, such as dimensioning, geometry and proportion, scale, movement and sequence, circulation and accessibility, public and private, morphology, topography, urban fabric and land use, etc.
outcome: Understanding of the fundamental concepts of measurement and how they apply to architecture and urban design. Ability to collect and analyse measurements to create scaled drawings and models, improving design representation skills and reflecting a nuanced understanding of architectural configuration and urban context. Ability to use appropriate representational media, including models and hand-drawn diagrams and projections. Ability to present architectural studies in various formats, including performances and films, enhancing storytelling and presentation skills. Ability to critically engage with architectural drawing archives, interpreting design information and addressing issues of scale and representation. Understanding of visual perception principles and the systems of order that inform architectural composition and urban design. Understanding of the design-build process through hands-on experiences. Awareness of the non-linear nature of the design process. Awareness of historical approaches to urban planning and measurement, such as the Nolli Plan, and how these methods can influence contemporary architectural practices. Awareness of the history of urban development in the Central area of Hong Kong and its relationship to current urban form and social dynamics. Awareness of the relationship between human behaviour and the physical environment, emphasising accessibility and inclusivity. Understanding the impact of buildings on the environment and the way in which buildings fit into their context Ability to document the design process effectively, reflecting on decision-making and evolving ideas through sketches and models. Ability to engage in reflective practice, learning from mistakes and refining designs based on feedback and teamwork. Ability to collaborate effectively with peers, sharing skills and perspectives to tackle complex challenges.

title: Introduction to Architectural Design II
requirements: Prerequisite: ARCH2111.
description: Introduction to Architectural Design I to II and Architectural Design Studio I to IV (ARCH2111, 2112, 3113, 3114, 4115, 4116) form a sequence of project-based professional courses in architecture.Studio 2 – PROTOTYPE (ARCH2112) subverts the conventional approach that design begins with a conceptual design idea to be only materialised and performed later; instead it places performance at the heart of design thinking. Throughout the semester, as they iterate between performing and building, they ultimately construct, activate, and film a building whose form is inseparable from the movements and actions it supports.
outcome: Understanding the core concepts of prototyping and their role in shaping architectural design and practice. Building up hands-on skills, testing materials, construction methods, and spatial ideas through iterative modelling and making. Learning a variety of representation techniques, including models, hand sketches, and film, to communicate design concepts and processes as they develop. Familiarity with design-build precedents, exploring how prototyping connects to construction and real-world user experience. Gaining practical experience in the design-build cycle by collaborating in teams, adapting to challenges and shifting opportunities on-site. Embracing and learning the experimental, non-linear nature of prototyping, taking risks and learning through discovery during every phase. Developing awareness of material lifecycles, sustainability strategies, and ways to design for future disassembly and reuse. Understanding how user actions and spatial configuration drive adaptability, accessibility, and collective participation. Awareness of environmental impacts, integrating sustainable choices in materials and methods within the project’s unique context. Learning how to document the entire design-build process, reflecting visually and narratively on decisions, evolving ideas, and teamwork. Learning how to collaborate effectively with peers, sharing ideas and skills to overcome complex design and construction challenges.

title: Digital Media
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH3222
description: Digital media introduces architecture students to core digital design and synthesis methods. Students develop essential skills in digital drafting, 3D modelling, techniques for digitization, and learning to move between analog and digitally driven workflows across different media. Students gain technical fluency and an understanding of how digital tools support contemporary architectural thinking and production processes.
outcome: Participants who complete this course will have a broad knowledge of various digital technology, design instruments, and techniques that they can use in architectural design. They will have sufficient practical skills allowing them to immediately apply in design studios and other courses.
syllabus: Digital design media, methods of communications, and design tools in architecture are the core topics addressed in this course. Digital instruments for drawing, drafting, image processing, 3D modelling and visualization, layout, video, and fabrication are introduced through lectures covering theoretical concepts and practical skill building exercises. These learning outcomes are applied and transferred to problems and situations arising from the Architectural Design Studio.

title: Architecture Fundamentals
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH4426
description: This course is to introduce basic issues in architecture. The course covers four main topics: space, habitation, construction and urbanization. Space is the main objective of architectural design. Habitation refers to basic issues relating to how people use space and interact with physical environment. Construction refers to structure, material, construction and tectonic expression. Urbanization refers to urban fabric and open space. Students gain knowledge about these four topics through observing, analysing and recording the specific phenomenon from the living environment. The course is conducted in parallel with the Introduction to Architectural Design I (Design Studio U1) (ARCH2111) in the same sequence so that design and study could enhance with each other.

title: Architectural History and Theory I: Asian Architecture
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH3321
description: This course stresses the importance of understanding the history and theory associated with architectural form and space. It will reach this goal by identifying and investigating historic works of architecture from China and other Asian cultures that survive to the present. These investigations, which will employ the methods that historians currently use to analyse architecture, will provide students with the means to study other building types and architectural dynamics in further courses ARCH3322 and ARCH3323 of the architectural history and theory sequence.

title: Cultural Contexts I
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH3322
description: This course is an introduction to the history and theory of Western architecture from Classical Greece to contemporary times. It is primarily concerned with four themes: (1) concepts of geometry and proportion, (2) concepts of architectural representation, (3) professionalism and the institutionalization of architecture, and (4) the relationship between architecture and engineering since the 19th century. Students will acquire fundamental knowledge and terms of reference in preparation for the subsequent courses ARCH2323 and ARCH3321 of the architectural history and theory sequence.
outcome: Students who completed this course will have a basic knowledge of a general outline of Western architecture, and develop detailed knowledge of some buildings and architects; an ability to formulate critique in writing and in visual presentation; an awareness of how to connect historical and theoretical knowledge to design.
syllabus: In this course, students will explore ideas and practices that shape our architectural heritage - from the Greek conception of ideal beauty to the nineteenth-century idea of time and history. This course attempts to understand how, in various times in the past, these ideas manifest themselves in intellectual and technical levels through individual works of art and architecture; and how ideas are connected across places, times, and types of works

title: Cultural Contexts II
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH4323
description: This course stresses the importance of understanding architectural history and theory with respect to culture and context. There is a specific focus on 20th-century and contemporary architects and buildings, a range of key architects’ philosophies and approaches and the invisible forces around architecture. This course also provides theoretical ground for the parallel design studio and examines architectural history and theory through that lens. Students will study architecture with respect to historical continuities and ruptures, as well as explore the unity of forms and diversity of spatial practices.
outcome: Students who completed this course will have a general understanding and appreciation of  fundamental ideas, movements and key figures and works of modern and contemporary architecture; an awareness of the broader contexts of Modernist history and culture; have good knowledge on selected buildings, architects and related writings through their course works; have a decent ability to interpret and critique works of modern architecture in writing; an awareness of the applicability of architectural history and theory to the tasks of design.
syllabus: Outlines the history and theory of modern architecture through significant works of the 20th century as well as some contemporary exemplars. Works of architecture are examined as artifacts of their time, and as designed objects in their own right and for their own qualities. Focus will be on how individual works relate to important manifestoes, critical and imaginative writings, parallel developments in their cultural, and intellectual historical contexts.

title: Building Technology I: Materials and Construction
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH3423
description: Technical knowledge of materials, construction, and structures is vital for any building endeavour. This foundation is rooted in traditional techniques and practical experience, while also adapting to the latest advancements in science and technology. This course aims to inspire students to discover the art of construction as a driving force in design and to recognise that the essence of a building lies in the poetry of its assembly. By expressing materials strategically, choreographing joints and connections, and celebrating structural logic, we can craft spaces that enrich the human experience.
outcome: 1. Ability to analyse the technical and tectonic implications of material choices and construction methods 2. Ability to compare the possibilities and limitations of different material systems 3. Ability to identify the primary structural systems in the built environment 4. Ability to describe the behaviour of a structure, including how it supports and delivers loads, achieves adequate stiffness, maintains stability, and develops internal forces 5. Ability to use appropriate representational media, such as models, drawings, diagrams, and photographs, to convey information and explain design decisions 6. Ability to work cooperatively with others in a team setting 7. Develop a comprehensive knowledge of building materials, their properties, and construction techniques 8. Familiarise with the characteristics and design considerations of form-active, vector-active, and section-active structural systems 9. Understand the principles of structural behaviour in withstanding gravity and lateral forces
syllabus: TOPIC 1: STRUCTURAL PRINCIPLES AND PRIMARY TYPES OF STRUCTURAL SYSTEMS IN ARCHITECTURE Understanding basic structural principles, fundamental structural systems (such as form-active, vecto-active, and section-active), and their physical performance characteristics is essential. This allows students to select the most appropriate system for a given architectural design and explore a wider range of design possibilities, creating more innovative, expressive, and efficient buildings. TOPIC 2: TECHNICAL ISSUES ASSOCIATED WITH MATERIALS AND CONSTRUCTION This refers to the practical, engineering-focused challenges that arise when selecting, specifying, and working with different building materials and construction methods. It encompasses considerations like structural integrity, load-bearing capacities, durability, and the technical processes involved in assembly and installation. Understanding these technical and tectonic issues is crucial for ensuring the structural safety, functional performance, and constructability of architectural designs. TOPIC 3: ISSUE OF SUSTAINABILITY AND INNOVATIVE BUILDING TECHNIQUES This refers to the need for architects to consider the environmental impact and energy efficiency of the materials and construction methods they specify. It involves understanding how innovative building techniques can contribute to more sustainable and energy-saving design solutions. Addressing these issues is crucial for creating buildings with reduced carbon footprint and operational energy demands.TOPIC 4: BUILDING TECHNOLOGY AND THE CREATION OF SPACE This speaks to how material selection, construction methods, and the design of the structural systems could work with spatial design to create a certain spatial experience and atmosphere. Addressing these issues is essential for translating the architect's intended experiential qualities of a space into the built environment. The dual technical and creative aspects of architecture include the need to rigorously address material and construction challenges while also masterfully designing meaningful, experiential spaces.

title: Building Technology II: Materials and Construction
description: This course focuses on fundamental knowledge and design methods for architectural structures. By revealing and analysing the internal forces within architectural structures through graphic statics, the course introduces the basic principles, systems, and materials of architectural structures in both qualitative and quantitative ways. The aim is to connect structural forms and forces through graphical methods, making structural design an essential element that enhances spatial form, rather than an obstacle to design.

title: Architectural Design Studio I
requirements: Prerequisite: ARCH2112.
description: Introduction to Architectural Design I to II and Architectural Design Studio I to IV (ARCH2111, 2112, 3113, 3114, 4115, 4116) form a sequence of project-based professional courses in architecture.Studio 3: ADAPT (ARCH3113) critically challenges the conventional myth of architectural permanence—the notion that buildings must remain immutable over time. Rather than viewing architectural adaptation as a passive compromise or a functional step backward, this studio reframes it as the most potent form of architectural agency. In an era defined by climate emergency and social fragmentation, the studio moves beyond reactive survival strategies. Instead, it advocates for a proactive practice that synthesizes cultural resonance with ecological intelligence, empowering architects to actively shape a resilient and transformative future.
outcome: Understanding of the need to critically review precedents relevant to the function, organization and technological strategy of design proposals.  Understanding the cultural, social and intellectual histories, theories and technologies that influence the design of buildings. Knowledge to apply the influence of history and theory on the spatial, social, and technological aspects of architecture. Knowledge to apply appropriate theoretical concepts to studio design projects, demonstrating a reflective and critical approach. Awareness of the theories and methods of inquiry that seek to show the relationship between human behaviour and the physical environment.     Understanding of the needs and aspirations of building users. Awareness of the impact of buildings on the environment, and the precepts of sustainable design. Awareness of the way in which buildings fit into their local context. Understanding of the methods of investigation and preparation of the brief for a design project.  Ability to use appropriate representational media, such as drawings, models, diagrams, charts, including computer technology, to convey essential design information at each stage of the programming and design process. Understanding of the fundamentals of visual perception and the principles and systems of order that inform two- and three-dimensional design, architectural composition, and urban design. (design-formal ordering systems). Ability to create architectural designs that satisfy both aesthetic and technical requirements. Ability to work cooperatively with others in a team setting. Ability to discuss architectural ideas with non-architects, to listen objectively to their opinions and to consider those opinions in designing. Ability to employ basic methods of data collection and analysis to inform all aspects of the programming and design process. Ability to speak and write effectively on subject matters contained in the professional curriculum in Chinese and / or English.

title: Architectural Design Studio II
requirements: Prerequisite: ARCH3113.
description: Introduction to Architectural Design I to II and Architectural Design Studio I to IV (ARCH2111, 2112, 3113, 3114, 4115, 4116) form a sequence of project-based professional courses in architecture.Studio 4 - MATERIALISE (ARCH3114) reimagines architectural design as a critical process where making is a tool for discovery, exploring how material form is influenced by tools, labor, and socio-economic pressures. The course includes an overseas field study to examine how local climate and resources shape spatial qualities. Each studio section focuses on a specific material foundation aligned with circular economy principles like upcycling and reuse, viewing sustainability as integral to how buildings adapt and reintegrate into material streams.
outcome: Ability to develop a conceptual and critical approach to architectural design that integrates aesthetic ambitions with technical requirements, demonstrated through iterative prototyping, material experimentation, and the development of a comprehensive building proposal grounded in site-specific conditions. Ability to respond to natural and built site characteristics by translating observations from the Kyoto field trip into informed design strategies that connect material investigations with programmatic and spatial decisions. Ability to use appropriate representational media—including hand drawings, digital drawings, physical models, diagrams, and photographic documentation—to communicate design intent and iterative development at all stages of the studio process. Understanding of the principles of structural behaviour as applied to material assemblies and their translation into architectural systems, demonstrated through prototyping, connection detailing, and structural modeling. Understanding of the principles, conventions, standards, and applications of construction materials and assemblies, explored through hands-on engagement with a declared material type, forming and assembly operations, and iterative refinement of tectonic systems. Understanding of the fundamentals of visual perception and systems of order as they relate to material expression, spatial composition, and the iterative design process, demonstrated through crafted prototypes and architectural proposals. Awareness of the theories and methods of inquiry that link human behavior to material and spatial conditions, informed by field observations and cultural analysis during the Kyoto study trip. Adequate knowledge to apply theoretical concepts to studio design projects, demonstrating a reflective and critical approach to material agency, cultural context, and iterative design thinking. Knowledge to creatively apply fine arts principles—such as composition, proportion, and visual narrative—to the conceptualization and representation of material-based design investigations and architectural proposals.

title: Digital Design Methods
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH2222
description: Computational design, as an approach to architecture, applies the science of design problem solving to space, analysis, representation, interactivity, and buildability in the real world. Understanding how to create, manage and manipulate data is of paramount importance for young designers entering into a digital industry. The ability to manipulate formulae is a powerful tool for digital designers. It is an invaluable asset in architectural expression and lays the foundation for building a set of dynamic drawing tools. This course guides students through the rudiments of computational design, and gradually builds up a vocabulary of operations necessary to control elements within a three-dimensional environment.

title: Architecture and Global Culture
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH2321
description: Architecture and Global Culture is a thematic history and theory course for advanced undergraduates. As the culmination of three-course sequence in architectural history and theory, it seeks to prepare the student to take a position in contemporary debates of a global nature, debates in which architects may ultimately serve a significant role.
outcome: Improve capacities in deep reading: you will be encouraged to read texts both critically and closely. What do they say, but also, what do they obscure or neglect? What positions do they present? What subtexts do they contain? And capacities for scholarly writing: How can you use established scientific genres to communicate your message? Where is the line between description and advocacy? Sharpen skills in contextual analysis: At what scale are you arguing? What is the regional/global divide in your argument? How does the Greater Bay Area affect the globe, and vice versa? Who is your present constituency, and who are the future generations who will be shaped by the forces you describe? Train historical reasoning: What is the genealogy of motifs that shape discourse today? How are they similar, and how do they differ, between China and the West? Identify cross-disciplinary implications: How does architecture intersect with other fields such as environmental science, sociology, politics, ethics and anthropology? Phrased differently: when is a building not a mere construction but a mistake, a social space, a cradle of politics, a crime, or a ritual? Practice representational strategies, in particular via architectural drawing. Develop critical thinking skills
syllabus: The syllabus of the course varies annually within the framework established by the general topic (Architecture and Global Culture). It will be specified at the start of each semester within the course outline.

title: Architectural History and Theory II: Western Architecture
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH2322
description: In this course, students will explore ideas and practices that shaped of our architectural heritage. From the Greek conception of ideal beauty to the nineteenth-century idea of time and history, intellectual formulations are both exciting and practical; they inspire us and give us techniques for work. In this course, we will attempt to understand how, in various times in the past, these ideas manifest themselves in architectural and technical levels through individual works of art and architecture; we will also see how ideas are connected across places, times, and types of works. Above all, this course conveys an urgent agenda to develop critical engagement with the present in thoughtful ways in our architectural and urban interventions.

title: Building Technology II: Building Structure

Examines the characteristics and performance of a few basic structural assemblies, such as trusses, arch and cable systems, and frames. title: Building Technology III: Environmental Technology
description: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of passive environmental design. It examines the effect on buildings and their occupants of environmental conditions of light, temperature, air movement and sound. Case studies are used to review both traditional and current approaches of representative building types in more depth.
outcome: Upon the completion of the course, students will have demonstrated basic understanding of fundamental issues related to the environmental design of architecture. They will acquire knowledge of the subject with sufficient exposure and at a suitable level so that they will be able to appreciate the topical issues of climate, human bio-meteorology and the design of indoor and outdoor environment for human habitation. This will allow the design of better buildings, further study, or to pursue a career in the building design and construction industry.
syllabus: Introduces the fundamental concepts of passive environmental design. Case studies are used to reviews both traditional and current approaches of representative building types in more depth.   • To understand the significances of environmental design in architecture. • To understand and to be able to apply appropriate environmental strategies in different climatic and urban contexts to achieve human comfort. • To have a basic understanding of the building physics related to passive environmental design. • To appreciate the application and integration of passive environmental design in architectural works. • To develop skills in conducting a systematic investigation into the subject and presenting the results in a clear and convincing manner.

title: Land and City
requirements: Not for students who have taken ARCH4721
description: This course introduces students to key theories and practices in the design of the built environment, emphasizing the reciprocal relationships between urban forms and the socio-economic and environmental processes that shape them. Through lectures, discussions, and local field trips, students will attain a historical perspective on the development of cultural landscapes across diverse geographical settings. Importantly, they will be encouraged to challenge preconceived notions while enhancing their critical thinking and writing skills in architectural and urban research.The course encompasses three interrelated aspects: (1) ‘Urban Morphology,’ which examines evolving discourses in planning, architecture and urban design; (2) ‘Urban Landscapes,’ focusing on the growing significance of landscape architecture in development; and (3) ‘Urban Sustainability,’ exploring theories and practices related to sustainable cities. Throughout the course, students will engage with emerging sustainability challenges of the 21st century.
outcome: Acquire fundamental knowledge of the principles of urban planning and design and how these practices have co-evolved with social, cultural, and economic processes from a historical perspective. Demonstrate a critical understanding of the complexity and interconnectedness of urban challenges by thinking across times and geographical scales. Understand the basic principles of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and connect them with planning and design practices, including the use and management of resources and their environmental and social impacts.   Become familiar with the intersections among various built environment disciplines, including planning, architecture, landscape architecture, and urban design.  Acquire knowledge of Hong Kong’s urban histories and their relationship with local, regional, and international development.   Develop critical thinking and analytical skills essential for architectural and urban research.
syllabus: This course offers a comprehensive introduction to major intellectual currents that underpin of contemporary planning and urban design, as well as the socio-economic and environmental processes that have shaped cultural landscapes across diverse geographical settings. Emphasis will be placed on connecting theory and practice through in-depth analysis of international and local case studies. The aim is to equip students with a critical understanding of the complex dynamics influencing the forms of the built environment while encouraging reflection on the multifaceted challenges faced by design professionals in historical and contemporary contexts.

title: Architectural Design Studio III
requirements: Prerequisite: ARCH3114.
description: Introduction to Architectural Design I to II and Architectural Design Studio I to IV (ARCH2111, 2112, 3113, 3114, 4115, 4116) form a sequence of project-based professional courses in architecture.Studio 5 - INHABIT (ARCH4115) defines "inhabiting" as a process where dwellers adapt and create meaning within their environment, focusing on the link between inhabitants and the poetic aspects of daily life. The course reframes affordable housing as an architectural strategy aimed at restoring dignity to individuals with limited economic resources. It explores various models and encourages innovation in development and resource conservation. The studio emphasizes balancing economic feasibility with design goals, positioning housing as a means to promote social equity and human dignity in a modern context.
outcome: To engage with the reading of the city and different urban conditions through disciplinary studies and analysis.  To develop a design project with specific programs that foster the community life and individual living, particularly considering the needs of different groups of people.  To examine the complexities implicit in resolving urban problems acquiring proficiency in working across different scales: from the city to the building, from building to the living unit.  To reflect on the critical challenge of the affordable housing by conceptualizing alternative forms of living, providing a sustainable architectural prototype.

title: Architectural Design Studio IV
requirements: Prerequisite: ARCH4115.
description: Introduction to Architectural Design I to II and Architectural Design Studio I to IV (ARCH2111, 2112, 3113, 3114, 4115, 4116) form a sequence of project-based professional courses in architecture.Studio 6 – PERFORM (ARCH4116) is a Design Thesis. It serves as the final milestone of the undergraduate architectural journey, marking the transition from guided learning to independent inquiry. Students are responsible for defining their own architectural challenges and positions that require the ability to identify a critical contemporary issue, research its background, and develop a unique professional voice.The Design Thesis is a project of high complexity that requires translating abstract theories into a solid, coherent architectural proposal. Students must navigate conflicting forces and layers, treating architecture as a sophisticated argument rather than just a simple building solution. By the end of the semester, students are expected to test their own design philosophy, delivering a deeply considered project that expresses their architectural intentions with clarity and conviction. This final work acts as a rigorous proof of their readiness for the professional world.
outcome: Integrated Design Synthesis: Develop a conceptually rigorous architectural project (up to schematic design) that synthesizes program requirements, site context, user needs, aesthetic intent, and technical considerations, demonstrating a critical and reflective design approach. Technical Systems Integration: Understand, assess, select, and integrate structural systems, building envelope systems, and building assemblies into a coherent design solution. Sustainable Design Principles: Selectively incorporate principles of sustainable design, such as low-carbon strategies, and green architecture (encompassing energy, water, materials, indoor environmental quality, and site ecology) to minimize environmental impact and enhance building performance. Human-Centered Design: Understand and address the diverse needs, health, safety, well-being, and aspirations of building users, including designing for accessibility and varying physical abilities. Contextual & Community Responsiveness: Analyze and respond to site characteristics (natural and built), local context, and the potential impact of the project on existing and proposed communities. Program Development & Briefing: Develop well-defined building briefs/programs of targeted scales/types, establishing clear client/user requirements and their appropriateness to site and context. Regulatory & Life Safety Compliance: Understand and apply relevant regulatory requirements, building codes, and the fundamental principles governing the design of life-safety systems and provisions. Effective Representation & Communication: Proficiently prepare, document, and present design proposals using appropriate representational media (drawings, models, diagrams, digital tools) and communicate complex architectural ideas clearly. Critical Evaluation & Analysis: Critically analyze, evaluate, and assess buildings, urban spaces, design proposals, and the completed project against program criteria, technical performance, and contextual fit. Research & Inquiry: Employ appropriate methods of research, data collection, analysis, and theoretical inquiry to inform programming, design decisions, and understanding of human behavior in relation to the physical environment.

description: The three-course sequence in architectural history and theory culminates in the analysis of architectural works produced in conjunction with changes in the 20th and 21st centuries. title: Building Systems Integration
description: After exposure to material and construction, building structures, and environmental technology, it is time for students to take these systems and considerations to shape their next studio project. Through the appreciation of finely integrated projects and examination of daily surroundings, students are encouraged to rethink the core value of integration to the practice of architectural design and appreciate the technical aspects that inform our design decisions and strengthen our scheme from the inside. The course “Building Systems Integration” aims to empower students to 1) acquire fundamental understanding towards building systems, 2) investigate system integrations through building information modelling (BIM), and 3) challenge the effectiveness and efficiency of the existing building designs. Through the process, students reflect on how building technologies can be integrated for the articulation of their design concepts and resultant spaces.
outcome: Students are exposed to the knowledge in the areas:1. The role of the architect within the design team and construction industry, recognizing the importance of current methods and trends in the construction of the built environment;2. Understand through investigation, how selection of alternative structural, constructional and material systems are relevant to architectural design;3. Strategies for building construction, and ability to integrate knowledge of structural principles and construction techniques;4. The physical properties and characteristics of building materials, components and systems, and the environmental impact of specification choices.5. Principles associated with designing optimum visual, thermal and acoustic environments;6. Strategies for building services, and ability to integrate these in a design project.7. Understand the cost control mechanisms which operate during the development of a project.
syllabus: This course is challenge-driven and student-led, as structured by a series of lectures, guest lectures, student presentations, field trips, hands-on workshops and project-based assignments. Project-based assignments include 1) Case studies, which equip students with the foundational knowledge regarding building systems and their integration with architecture, 2) BIM studies, and 3) Redesign proposals. In-class training by BIM expert will be arranged. The level of difficulty increases progressively from Assignment 1 to 3 and will align with studio teaching to maximise the learning outcomes from the students’ perspective. Tutorials will be arranged to have in-depth discussions with students in group formats.

description: This course introduces students to important theories and practices associated with the urban built environment that affects and is affected by various socioeconomic and environmental processes. It provides an understanding of the physical aspects of the city around and beyond architecture to allow the students to think critically about the spatial phenomena of contemporary urbanism. By reading and analyzing various components of the urban built environment, students learn to develop systematic approaches to understanding the relationship between spatial design and the city holistically across multiple spatial scales. title: Architectural Theory and Criticism
requirements: For students in Master of Architecture
description: This is a challenging course designed to re-acquaint master’s students with writing as a reflective practice, as a means of communication, and as a scientific resource. Like drawing, writing is a fundamental tool of architecture. It is also a practice. Both free writing—where one just observes and remarks on experiences—and research writing—where one carefully formulates questions, compiles supporting information, evaluates it, presents a case, and draws conclusions—will be required of students. All tools, from site and archival visits, to critical drawing and AI, are woven into the research examples. LLMs are introduced as a research and interrogation tool, but the use of AI to generate prose is discouraged. Master’s students will be ready to write a dissertation and perhaps even pursue additional post-graduate research with the help of this course.
outcome: - Able to analyze critical writing and buildings, and to draw out the ideas behind them. - Able to discuss major concepts of architectural theory and criticism from the mid twentieth century. - Able to complement the design studio through the influential projects and ideas discussed in class.

title: Urban History and Theory
requirements: For students in Master of Architecture and MSc in Urban Design;Mutually exclusive to URBD5703
description: This course examines the main ideas, histories and theories of the city through specific local and international examples from significant historical, political, geographical and environmental periods and aspects. Important themes and debates in urban design and planning will be critically explored to understand the relationship between the urban forms, the culture of cities and their sustainable development. In particular, the way urban forms have been used and reinterpreted, adapted and challenged by different social, economic and political contexts. Exemplary design projects and planning policies are investigated in view of their relationship to contexts and their impacts on communities and the environment.
outcome: The course aims to familiarize students with the histories and theories of urbanism and the role of design in shaping city forms and social environments. It seeks to equip students with knowledge of city planning, design, and development policy, as well as the needs and aspirations of local communities. Through in-class discussions and debates, students are encouraged to challenge their preconceived assumptions and analyse various urban issues from comparative perspectives. The learning process will also help them develop critical thinking and academic writing skills relevant to research in architecture and urban studies. Students are allowed to use AI tools in some learning activities as specified in the individual assignment handouts. In such cases, they are required to explicitly acknowledge the use of these tools, and must document the specific tools used, how they were employed, their assessment of the feedback received from the tools and whether the feedback was incorporated into their submitted work.
syllabus: The course familiarizes students with various methods for studying cities as pursued in the social sciences and humanities, including history, geography, and urban studies. Through in-depth discussion and debates of selected case studies, students will gain a historical perspective of urbanization and develop the ability to analyze specific urban issues, identifying continuities and congruences in city development across different time periods and locations.  This course aligns with the framework of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the UN Habitat’s Urban Agenda, emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary thinking to address today’s pressing urban challenges. A major assignment will require students to explore the concepts of the SDGs and establish meaningful connections with contemporary design practice in Hong Kong.

title: Introduction to Architectural Conservation
requirements: For students in Master of Architecture
description: The history of a locality is often defined by its culture and the built manifestations of that culture. The preservation of the architectural heritage of a culture is an indication of the importance that culture placed on its past. The trend in the developed world today is to preserve historical monuments, historic district, tangible and intangible heritage as much as possible. In Asia, conservation has a checkered history. For China and Hong Kong, architectural conservation is at the early stages of development. Much have been learned and much have to be done. This course is designed to introduce the basic concepts and practices in conservation with a particular emphasis on conservation practices in Hong Kong and the region. It will serve as the foundation for further development of interest and skill in conservation.

title: Materials and Construction in Architectural Conservation
requirements: For students in Master of Architecture
description: Every building tradition has its unique construction system employing primarily local materials and craftsmanship. This course will introduce to the students various regional traditions, such as the timber tradition in East Asia, stone and brick tradition both ingenious and imported to East Asia and the 20th century tradition in the region with local and imported materials. Issues and techniques in employing these materials and construction systems in historic periods will be addressed. Site visit will be a feature of this course.

title: Issues in Heritage Conservation
requirements: For students in Master of Architecture
description: This course will address the pertinent and current issues facing heritage conservation in the region. The format will be a heritage forum with invited speakers articulating the current discourses and issues which might include conservation legislature frameworks, cultural values of built heritage, grass-root advocacy, heritage tourism, sustainability, revitalization of heritage sites, or issues facing specific projects in urban renewal, conservation of national monuments, and other design projects. The key activities of the course are discussions and dialogues for understanding and critique of the current practices in conservation of built heritage in Hong Kong, China and the region, as well as to explore the future.

title: Hong Kong Architectural History (Culture of Building)
requirements: For students in Master of Architecture
description: This course looks at the architectural development and planning in Hong Kong through historical periods, examining both traditional Chinese settlements and colonial urban development. Issues such as culture and society, land and building regulations, rural and urban conditions, as well as building techniques will be covered. At the end of the course, student shall be able to identify the architectural style, spatial quality, layout, function, and decoration of buildings of different types and periods. The types of buildings that will be covered include the following three categories:- Chinese traditional buildings;- Buildings with colonial influence from late nineteenth to early twentieth centuries;- Building with modern building technique from 1910-1970

title: Visual Studies
description: The course introduces the visual arts and examines how its history and ideas can help develop our critical understanding of spatial design. The course offers an overview of the subject for those with little or no art background and is intended to provide a sense of visual literacy. The course is designed to awaken your skills of observation, interpretation and creativity, as well as giving you a strong intellectual grounding in visual thinking, and the form, meaning and content of visual art.
outcome: • Demonstrate a familiarity with major historical movements in art and be able to explain how art relates to its time and culture. • Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the elements of art, principles of design, and the creative process.  • Demonstrate an understanding and awareness of the various art media. • Demonstrate an appreciation of the role of art in society as a means to expand their outlook and develop the expression of their own ideas in various visual media and forms.
syllabus: The course consists of 9 topics arranged in three groups in terms of drawing media: line, tone and color. The first group focuses on three basic formal elements as shape, volume and space in addition to basic drawing systems. The second group focuses on figure and ground relationship, light and shade, and plasticity. The third group focuses on abstract color, perceived color and texture.
required_readings: 1. Douglas Cooper, Drawing and perceiving, Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1992 2. Gu Daqing, Design and Visual Perception, China Architecture and Building Press, 2002 3. Frank Ching, Drawing a creative process, Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1990 4. Betty Edwards, Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain, Fontana, 1982 5. Kimon Nicolaides, The Natural Way to Draw, Houghton Mifflin Company Boston, 1941 6. Claudia Betti and Teel Sale, Drawing —A Contemporary Approach, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich College Publication, 1992
